buckingmill-handbook-assembly-text: Place the frame where the whole machine has room: it is six blocks long, three wide and four high, and runs away from you, with the block you place as the middle of its near end. The far end takes the axle and the trunks; the logs come out of the near end. Then fit Immersive Woodworking's sawmill parts with rightmouse, in any order: two saw sashes, a crankshaft, feed levers and a blade kit, which puts a blade in each saw, so it goes in after both sashes. No carriage is needed. The crankshaft strokes the two saws back and forth across the trunk, and they sink through it under their own weight. When they reach the bottom they trip the levers, which engage a windlass that winds them back up on ropes; at the top the carriage trips the levers back, the windlass lets go, and they start down again. While it is turning the mill never stops: with no trunk on the bed the saws keep going up and down. ctrl + rightmouse takes the blade kit back out. The other parts come back only when you break the frame, which drops every fitted part. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on an unassembled mill fits its next part, as on the woodworking stations, with nothing taken from you.
buckingmill-handbook-power-text: Connect a turning axle to the far end of the mill, high up, where the shaft ends (the top of the end, in the middle). The assembled mill is a heavy load, twice a plank sawmill's, and it only cuts while its shaft turns at a fair speed. Until it is assembled it barely loads the shaft.
buckingmill-handbook-trunks-text: The mill cuts Logging Expanded tree trunks of any size, one at a time. Trunks must have their branches removed first while Logging Expanded asks for that. On the bed every one-block-thick trunk looks the same, four blocks long, and every two-block-thick one five blocks long, whatever its own length; the trunk you take back out is the one you loaded. Carry a trunk on your shoulder and hold rightmouse on the mill to load it. It goes on when the saws are at the top of their cycle: if they are not, keep the button held and it goes on as they come up. A trunk storage rack feeds the running mill. Stand it on the ground right against the mill's far end, under the axle, at the level of the block you placed the mill on: one of its two blocks must be in one of the three blocks just beyond that end, and it may run either way, in line with the bed or across it. The mill takes the rack's top trunk whenever the bed is empty and the saws come round to the top. A branched trunk on top of the rack holds the line until you deal with it. The mill's info says what the rack offers, or why nothing is coming. With no rack or rosser there ready, the mill takes a trunk lying on the ground in those three blocks, its middle in one of them, the same way. A rosser feeds the mill as a rack does: place the rosser on the block just beyond the mill's far end, in line with its middle, looking the way you looked when you placed the mill. The mill takes each debarked trunk off it when the bed is empty and the saws come to the top, and a debarked trunk gives debarked logs. ctrl + rightmouse takes the trunk back out onto your shoulder, but only before a quarter of it is cut.
buckingmill-handbook-yield-text:
Every log stored in a trunk takes 8 turns of the shaft with copper blades, and gives 2 logs of its wood, which slide off the rails at the near end. A cut trunk's resin and branches are lost, as on a sawhorse.

After each cut the saws wind back up to the top, which takes 6 turns of the shaft from the bottom; with no trunk they take another 6 to come down, so an empty cycle is 12 turns. A trunk taken back out early lets them carry on down from where they are. The next trunk can only go on while they are at the top.

Better blades cut faster, by their metal's tool tier: bronze about 1.35 times as fast as copper, iron 1.7 times and steel about twice (gold and silver no faster than copper). Only the cut is faster; the saws go up and down empty at the same speed whatever the blades.

The blade kit loses 1 durability for every log stored in a cut trunk. A worn out kit breaks and the mill stops, its saws where they are, until a new one is fitted.

A mill that stops turning leaves its saws where they are. While it is stopped, hold <hk>rightmouse</hk> on it with an empty hand to wind them up to the top by hand; a trunk on the bed stays, and when the mill turns again the saws come back down onto it where the cut had got to. These figures are the defaults of BuckingSawmillSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.

rosser-handbook-assembly-text: Place the frame where the whole machine has room: it is sixteen blocks long, five wide and four high, and runs away from you, with the block you place as the middle of its near end. Trunks go in at the far end and come out debarked at the near end. Then fit its parts with rightmouse, in any order, except that the tyres and the scraper heads go on the ring: a sawmill crankshaft for the drive, four large gear sections for the toothed ring, two hoops for its tyres, four rods for the infeed and outfeed rolls, two metal plates for the limb breaker, sawmill feed levers for the treadle and the feed's levers, and four bark spud heads of one metal for the scraper tips. Hoops, rods and plates must be iron, meteoric iron or steel, as the woodworking machines' parts are; the heads may be any metal. A click fits as many as the part still needs from the stack in your hand, and four rods fill both sets of rolls. With no trunk in it, ctrl + rightmouse takes unused heads back out. The other parts come back only when you break the frame, which drops every fitted part (the heads only if unused) and the trunk. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on an unassembled rosser fits its next part, as on the woodworking stations, with nothing taken from you.
rosser-handbook-power-text:
Connect a turning axle to the rosser's right-hand side as you look along it from its near end: to the top block of that side, ten blocks back from the near end, beside the ring. It may turn either way. The assembled rosser is a heavy load, and it only feeds while its shaft turns at a fair speed; the ring spins whenever the shaft turns.

Water is optional. A Pipes and Power Expanded water pipe against the other side, on the third block up, nine blocks back from the near end, fills a small reservoir that drips onto the trunk just ahead of the ring. A full reservoir wets ten logs. Each wet log gives half as many pieces of bark again, and the special kinds of bark more often.
rosser-handbook-trunks-text: The rosser takes Logging Expanded tree trunks of any size, branched or not, one at a time. On the beds every one-block-thick trunk looks the same, four blocks long, and every two-block-thick one five blocks long, whatever its own length. It does not take trunks that are already debarked. Carry a trunk on your shoulder and hold rightmouse on the rosser to load it. It goes onto the infeed bed at the far end, and its weight on the treadle starts the feed as soon as the shaft turns. The rolls draw it through the limb breaker, which snaps off its branches, and the spinning ring, whose scrapers take off its bark, onto the outfeed bed. A trunk storage rack feeds the running rosser its top trunk whenever it is empty. Stand it on the ground right against the far end: one of its two blocks must be in one of the three blocks just beyond that end. A debarked trunk on top of the rack holds the line until you take it off. With no rack there ready, the rosser takes a trunk lying on the ground in those three blocks, its middle in one of them, the same way. A rack stood the same way against the near end takes each debarked trunk while it has room for it; a full one leaves the trunk on the bed until there is room. A bucking sawmill takes the debarked trunk straight onto its bed when its saws come to the top. Place the mill first, then place the rosser on the block just beyond the mill's far end, in line with its middle, looking the same way. Otherwise the trunk waits on the outfeed bed. ctrl + rightmouse takes the trunk back onto your shoulder while it waits on either bed, but not while it is in the rolls.
rosser-handbook-yield-text:
Branches come off as sticks, one for every two branches, at the chute on the side away from the axle, as the trunk goes through the limb breaker. Bark comes off at the ring, log by log: Immersive Woodworking's bark for the trunk's wood, as a bark spud gives it. With water, each log's bark is half as much again and the better kinds are more likely.

The feed is geared, so every thin trunk goes through at one speed and every thick one at a slower one: with copper heads a thin trunk takes about 68 turns of the shaft and a thick one about 169. Better heads feed faster, by their metal's tool tier: bronze about 1.35 times as fast as copper, iron 1.7 times and steel about twice.

The four heads together last four times as long as a bark spud of their metal, losing one point for every log stored in a debarked trunk. Worn out heads break and the rosser stops until new ones are fitted. These figures are the defaults of RosserSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.

machineoil-text: The heavy machines need oil: the helve hammer, the pulverizer, the draw bench, the automated sawmill, the powered chopper, the bucking sawmill, the rosser and the gear cutter. The quern, axles, gears and the other transmission parts do not. Dry A machine is built dry, and runs dry again once its oil is used up. A dry machine works as well as an oiled one, but it takes three times the power to turn: on a windmill or water wheel that is already working hard, it can slow the whole network or stall it. It smokes while it turns. Any oil at all in the tank, however little, and it turns as easily as ever. Oiling Hold a bucket, jug or bowl of oil and press rightmouse on any part of the machine: as much as fits goes in, and the rest stays in the container. Holding oil, the click always pours, whatever else it would have done there. Lumps of rendered fat go in the same way, half a litre each. The oils: flax and olive oil, every Expanded Foods cooking oil (seed, nut, olive, rice bran and the rest), and lard, liquid or hardened. Oil cannot be taken back out, and breaking the machine loses it. How long it lasts The tank holds 1000 points, 100 to the litre: one full bucket. Only work uses oil, never turning idle: a helve hammer a tenth of a point for each strike on an anvil with work on it, a pulverizer half a point an item, the draw bench 2 points a pipe section drawn (8 a tube blank), the sawmill 2 points a log, the chopper 1 point a log, and the bucking sawmill and the rosser 2 points for each log stored in a trunk, and the gear cutter 10 points a gear (20 a large one). The gear cutter is the exception to the dry rule: dry or oiled it takes the same power, but its oil spares its cutter kit, which wears faster as the tank runs down and breaks on the first gear cut dry. A full tank lasts days of steady work. Look at the machine to see how much is left, and the load it puts on its shaft in kN, the same scale as a windmill's power output.

woodworking-overview-text: Wood leaves the forest as tree trunks. You turn them into logs, boards, support beams, firewood and bark at a few stations, each built in the world. The chapters below follow them in the order you will need them. 1. Trunks A felled tree leaves one tree trunk on the ground holding all its logs. Take it by one end and move it where you need it, or carry it on your shoulder to a station. Cut its branches off with a knife. An axe or a saw gets wood out of a trunk on the ground, but wastefully: an axe gives one log for every two the trunk holds. 2. Sawhorses A primitive sawhorse, built from sticks and rope, takes every log out of a trunk, and saws logs into boards or support beams. Standard and advanced sawhorses saw more boards per log. 3. Splitting block Right-click an upright log with an axe to make a splitting block. Chop logs on it into firewood, and firewood into sticks. Upgraded with iron, it gives more firewood per log. 4. Bark Debarking logs on a sawhorse, or debarking a splitting block, gives bark: tanning bark for tannin, birch bark for tar, bast for rope, medicinal bark for poultices. 5. Machines With mechanical power, an automated sawmill saws logs and an automated chopper splits them for you.
woodworking-trunks-text: Felling A felled tree leaves a tree trunk lying on the ground rather than loose logs. The trunk holds every log of the tree and, until you cut them off, its branches. Pine and acacia trunks also hold resin. A trunk fits in no bag or chest: work it where it lies, or move it. Moving a trunk Press rightmouse near one end of a trunk with an empty hand to take that end. You stand beyond that end facing along it, like pushing a sled: walkforward pushes the trunk ahead of you, walkbackward draws it back as you walk backwards, and walkleft and walkright swing it round its middle. Press sneak to let go. The more logs it holds, the slower it moves: a trunk of 48 logs moves at half a walk. No one else can touch a trunk you are moving. Tie a rope to it to tow it behind an animal or a cart, or to tie it to a post. Walking into a trunk shoves it, and trunks float. To load a station, shoulder the trunk with shift + rightmouse and an empty hand. You walk very slowly while you carry it, slower the more logs it holds. Hold rightmouse on a sawhorse, a storage or heating rack, a rosser or a bucking sawmill to load it, or on a cart's or sled's storage to stow it. Put it down on the ground as you put down anything you carry. A trunk you take back off any of them goes onto your shoulder. Debranching Hold rightmouse on a branchy trunk with a knife. Each 2-second hold cuts off up to 12 branches and gives a stick for each. A trunk with branches left can't be worked with an axe or a saw, or loaded on a sawhorse. With shears instead, a hold turns 12 branches into a sapling. Working a trunk on the ground Hold rightmouse with an axe to take off one log for every two the trunk holds, or with a saw to cut 6 boards per log. With a hammer in your offhand, the axe gives debarked logs at the same rate, but no bark. A bark spud held on a trunk with no branches debarks the whole trunk in one long hold, half a second per log, and drops each log's bark. Working a trunk on the ground wastes wood: load it on a sawhorse as soon as you can. Storage and resin A trunk storage rack holds 4 trunks. A trunk heating rack over a fire drains the resin from pine and acacia trunks. A stick storage holds up to 128 sticks. Their pages say how to build them. Next: Sawhorses. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-sawhorses-text: Sawhorses take logs out of trunks and saw them into boards and support beams. There are three, each better than the last, all built in the world. Primitive sawhorse Put exactly 18 sticks in a pile on the ground and right-click the pile with a knife: it becomes a large stick frame. Hold rightmouse on the frame with 4 rope to finish the sawhorse. Standard sawhorse Put exactly 36 boards of one wood in a pile and right-click it with a hammer to make a board frame. Add 2 debarked logs, then hold rightmouse with 20 copper or bronze nails and strips in your hand and a hammer in your offhand. The sawhorse is of the boards' wood and the nails' metal. Advanced sawhorse Make a board frame and add 2 debarked logs, as above. Then add 2 iron plates and 4 iron rods, and hold rightmouse with 20 iron nails and strips and a hammer in your offhand to finish the advanced sawhorse. Loading Carry a debranched trunk to a sawhorse on your shoulder and hold rightmouse on it to load the trunk (see Trunks), or right-click it with up to 16 logs of one wood. Right-click a loaded sawhorse with empty hands to take the load back: a trunk onto your shoulder, logs into your inventory. A sawhorse takes only logs with their bark on. Working Each hold of rightmouse, under a second, works one log and costs the tool 1 durability: • An axe takes off a log. • A saw cuts boards: 9 per log on the primitive sawhorse, 12 on the standard, 18 on the advanced. • A saw with shift held cuts support beams: 2 per log on the primitive and standard sawhorse, 3 on the advanced. • A bark spud, or an axe with a hammer in your offhand, gives a debarked log and drops that log's bark. From a trunk, the advanced sawhorse works 2 logs per hold with an axe, with or without a hammer, and with a bark spud, and gives 3 logs for them: the axe still loses 1 durability, a bark spud 2. Breaking a sawhorse drops its load and gives back about three quarters of what it took to build. Next: Splitting block. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-splittingblock-text: Making one Place a log upright and right-click it with an axe: the log becomes a splitting block of its wood, for 1 durability. There is no crafting recipe. Breaking a splitting block gives it back, with its wood and upgrades. Chopping Put a log on the block with rightmouse, then hold rightmouse with an axe: • a log splits into 2 half-logs; • put a half-log back and it splits into 3 firewood, or 4 on an advanced block; • firewood goes on the block too, and splits into 2 sticks. So a log gives 6 firewood, or 8 on an advanced block. A maul splits a whole log into firewood in one pass, at the same yield. Debarked logs split the same way; quarter logs split straight into firewood. Take wood back off the block with ctrl + rightmouse. shift + rightmouse with an axe leaves the axe stuck in the block until you take it back the same way. Upgrades Upgrade an empty block, without shift or ctrl, in this order: 1. Debarked: hold rightmouse with a bark spud, or with an axe and a hammer in your offhand, as long as stripping a log takes. The block's bark drops on top. 2. Bound: right-click with 2 iron hoops. 3. Advanced: hold rightmouse for 3 seconds with 8 iron nails and strips and a hammer in your offhand. Debarked and bound blocks chop like a new one, 6 firewood per log. The advanced block gives 8, and only an advanced block can be the bed of an automated chopper. Next: Bark. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-bark-text: Getting bark Bark comes off logs in three places: • on a sawhorse, debarking with a bark spud or an axe with a hammer in your offhand: bark for every log debarked; • on a splitting block, when you debark the block itself: bark for one log; • on a trunk on the ground, with a bark spud, which debarks the whole trunk at once: bark for every log it holds. An axe with a hammer in your offhand on a trunk on the ground gives debarked logs, but no bark. Which bark Each debarked log gives 3 pieces of one kind of bark, chosen by chance from its wood; otherwise it is ordinary bark. A log's handbook page lists the chances under "When stripped". Oak, acacia and larch are good for tanning bark, birch for birch bark, bald cypress and redwood for bast, kapok and ebony for medicinal bark. A bark spud finds the special kinds more often than an axe and hammer, and a spud of better metal more often still. Uses • Tanning bark: soak it in a barrel of water for weak tannin, or in weak tannin for strong tannin. Dried bark soaks faster, and crushed bark (dried bark ground on a quern) faster still. • Birch bark: pack it into a perforated pot set on an empty clay pot, seal it with clay and fire it in a pit kiln for birch tar, which stands in for resin. • Bast: 6 make a rope on the crafting grid. It also makes poultices. • Medicinal bark: simmer it in a pot with water for bark decoction, for healing poultices. • Ordinary bark: fuel for a pit kiln in place of sticks, and compost in a barrel. Next: Machines. Back to Woodworking.
woodworking-machines-text: Both machines run on mechanical power: connect an axle from a windmill or water wheel. Each is a frame you craft (it needs support beams; its page shows the recipe), place, and complete by installing its parts with rightmouse, in any order. Only the blade kit or the head can be taken back out, with ctrl + rightmouse; break the frame to recover the other parts. Automated sawmill Install a carriage, a saw sash, a crankshaft and feed levers, then a blade kit in the sash. Feed it logs or debarked logs, by hand or through a chute. By default a log comes out as 24 boards and a debarked log as 6 support beams; shift + rightmouse on the frame switches to boards only or beams only. Automated chopper Install a drive, an arm and an advanced splitting block as the bed, then a chopper head in the arm. A splitting block that is not advanced is refused, so upgrade it first. Load it with logs or firewood, by hand or through a chute. A log comes out as 8 firewood in one pass, and firewood as sticks. Breaking the frame gives the advanced splitting block back. Back to Woodworking.

game:itemdesc-gear-rusty: Despite its corroded state, it still shows exceptional quality and craftsmanship. The fine details seem impossible to reproduce. Probably why the traders favor it so much. Under the corrosion it is stainless steel, which does not rust on its own: the Rust ate it.
gearreclamation-rusty-text: Stainless steel, corroded by the Rust: stainless does not rust on its own. Degrease, pickle, passivate, neutralize. One in ten comes out sound. See Gears.
gearreclamation-section-text: Part of the gear chain: rusty gears reclaimed (boil, pickle, passivate, neutralize; one in ten comes out sound), and stainless gears cut from blanks on the gear cutter. See Gears.
gearreclamation-large-text: The large gear machines want, cut from a large blank on the gear cutter with the large temporal gear as the master. See Gears.
gearreclamation-text: The rusty gears found in ruins are stainless steel. Stainless does not rust on its own: these were eaten by the Rust's incursion into the world, and by whatever the Jonas devices did to time around them. So they are salvage, and money every trader takes, but nothing is built from one. A machine that wants a gear wants a sound stainless gear. There are two ways to one: reclaim rusty gears, which is chemistry and mostly scrap, or cut new ones from stainless blanks on the gear cutter. Reclaiming: why each step The corrosion is a scale of oxide over the metal, and acid dissolves it faster than the steel under it. The line cleans the gear, takes the scale off, gives the steel back the thin chromium oxide skin that keeps stainless stainless, and washes the acid away. 1. Degrease Old grease keeps the acid off whatever it covers, so a greasy gear pickles in patches. Boil the gears off in a cooking pot over a fire with an alkali: Oils Resoaped's lye, or Expanded Matter's caustic soda or washing soda, a quarter litre for every gear, the gears in one, two or three slots of the pot, the same number in each. It is the only hot step. They come out degreased, still corroded. 2. Pickle Put the degreased gears in dilute acid in a pickling tub, a batch of up to 8, until the metal looks grey and clean. The weaker the acid, the longer it takes: vinegar about a day, sulfuric acid about 8 hours, Expanded Matter's hydrochloric acid about 2. A finished batch uses up a litre. Then take them out: once the scale is gone the acid starts on the steel itself, and past a grace of half the pickling time it eats the batch to stainless bits, a gear at a time, quickest in the strongest acid. They come out pickled: bare metal, its surface raw. 3. Passivate A raw surface has free iron in it and would stain. Put the pickled gears back in a pickling tub, in Expanded Matter's nitric acid this time, for about 6 hours: the acid takes the free iron off, and the chromium forms its passive skin again. Past a grace of 3 hours the nitric acid eats the batch too, a gear an hour. They come out passivated. 4. Neutralize Acid left on the metal keeps working. Seal the passivated gears in a barrel with lime water, a tenth of a litre a gear, for 2 hours, to stop it and rinse them. They come out neutralized, stainless again, and keep as long as you like: there is no hurry between the steps. One in ten Old gears are worn, pitted and cracked, and the acids show it. The moment you take neutralized gears into your inventory each one is decided: one in ten is a sound stainless gear, and each of the rest is a stainless steel bit, which goes back into a melting pot to be cast again. Blanks A cut gear starts as a blank: a stainless steel disc with a bore. Cast stainless gear blanks by pouring molten stainless steel into a fired gear blank mold (or set the mold on Steelmaking Expanded's canal pedestal), 25 units a blank, four to an ingot; or smith them at a steel anvil, two from a stainless steel ingot. A large gear blank takes 200 units, two ingots, in a large gear blank mold, or two ingots at the anvil. The molds take stainless steel only. The gear cutter The gear cutter is an automatic index miller of the 1870s, run by mechanical power. Its formed cutter mills one tooth gap, the table lifts the blank clear, a ratchet turns the blank on by one tooth, and it repeats until the gear is cut. The hard part of that was always the dividing, and here it is the part no one can make. Place the frame (eight steel ingots, planks, nails and strips, and three stainless gears for its own gearing), then fit its parts in order: the cutter spindle with its cone pulley, the feed screw, two Jonas eccentric gearboxes for the feed cam and the index cam (an eccentric is a cam, and the drums are the machine's programme), the lift cam, the index, a Jonas injection valve as the oiler, the dividing head (a Jonas planetary gear or difference gear assembly), the cutter kit, and the master. The master is a temporal gear: it rolls with the blank against a rack and gives the teeth their form, the one gear in the world with a perfect one. It is kept, never used up, and only one is fitted at a time: the temporal gear cuts 12-tooth stainless gears from small blanks, a large temporal gear 20-tooth large stainless gears from large blanks. Each tooth takes 12 turns of the axle: 144 for a gear, 240 for a large one. Keep the oiler's cup filled with machine oil. The cutter kit wears with every gear, and the emptier the cup the faster: at half full, twice as fast; dry, it breaks on the next gear.

picklingtub-handbook-text: The tub holds one liquid and one batch of up to 8 gears. Pour the liquid in with a bucket or jug, right-click with gears to add them, and right-click with an empty hand to take the batch out. An empty bucket takes the liquid back out. A batch uses up a litre of the liquid when it is done; taken out early, it gives the gears back unchanged and the litre goes back into the tub. Adding gears to a running batch starts it again. Pickling. Degreased gears go into dilute acid, one part acid to ten of water, until the metal looks grey and clean: vinegar takes about a day, sulfuric acid about 8 hours, hydrochloric acid about 2. Then take them out: past a grace of half the pickling time the acid starts on the steel and eats the batch to stainless bits, one gear at a time, quickest in the strongest acid. Check on it every few minutes. Passivating. Pickled gears go into nitric acid for about 6 hours, until the surface has gone passive. Past a grace of 3 hours the nitric acid eats them too, a gear an hour. Large gears are cut new, never reclaimed, and do not go in the tub.
itemdesc-steelbitcharge: Twenty steel bits packed together. In a stone coffin it takes an iron ingot's place, and comes out a blister steel ingot.
steelbits-error-few: Each ingot's place takes {0} steel bits
steelbits-handbook-text: Steel bits melt at 1502 °C, hotter than any fuel burns (coke reaches 1340 °C), so no forge or crucible melts them. Two ways take them back into steel. Cementation furnace In a stone coffin, 20 steel bits take the place of one iron ingot. Hold at least 20 and press shift + rightmouse on the coffin where an ingot would go: 20 bits go in, packed as one. A full coffin holds 16 such places, 320 bits, between its 5 layers of coke or charcoal, and is fired as for iron; it gives 16 blister steel ingots. Bits and iron ingots cannot share a coffin. Bits can also be packed beforehand, 20 at a time in the crafting grid, into packed steel bits, which go in the same way. Bessemer converter Steelmaking Expanded's Bessemer converter takes steel bits as cold scrap: holding them, press rightmouse on the vessel's upper hatch to charge them in with a raw iron charge, before the blow. Each bit is 5 units of steel, a twentieth of an ingot, and comes out as steel with the rest of the heat; each also cools the bath by 4 °C, which harder blast buys back.
handpump-handbook-title: On Pipes and Power Expanded's pipes
handpump-handbook-text: The hand pump finds its wellspring through Pipes and Power Expanded's pipes; Hydrate or Diedrate's own pipes and shut-off valves are no longer made, and any left in a world are removed as it loads, with nothing given back. Stand the pump on a pipe whose end opens upward into it (a vertical straight pipe, a bend or a junction; turn one with a wrench). The pump looks through every pipe joined to that one, of any metal and through open valves, for a wellspring beside any of them, or right under the pump. A closed valve cuts it off. A pipe may run straight down a well's shaft to its spring: the shaft still counts and holds water around it. The run must be empty or hold water: a run carrying steam, exhaust or air reaches no well. Priming takes one stroke for every 3 pipes between the pump and the spring (Hydrate or Diedrate's HandPumpPrimingBlocksPerStroke setting). The pipes carry none of the water: each stroke takes 2 liters straight from the spring, so the pump works beside water, steam or engines on other runs. A pipe end against the pump's underside or against a wellspring is sealed and leaks nothing. A Pipes and Power Expanded fluid intake over a well's water draws from the same spring, and gives no more than the spring holds: a well is a finite source for pipes too. The pump is made with two straight copper or lead pipes of its metal.
itemdesc-gearblank-*: A stainless steel disc with a bore, the size of a rusty gear: stock for cutting a gear.
seraphhorizons:item-handbooktext-seraphh: Cast it in a fired gear blank mold: pour 25 units of molten stainless steel into it, a quarter of an ingot, or set the mold on Steelmaking Expanded's canal pedestal, and take the blank out once it has hardened. Or smith two at a steel anvil from one stainless steel ingot; the helve hammer forges them as it forges a plate. A gear blank mold takes stainless steel only.
itemdesc-largegearblank-*: A stainless steel disc with a bore, the size of a large temporal gear: stock for cutting a large gear.
seraphhorizons:item-handbooktext-seraphh: Cast one in a fired large gear blank mold: pour 200 units of molten stainless steel (two ingots) into it, or set the mold on Steelmaking Expanded's canal pedestal, and take the blank out once it has hardened. Or smith one at a steel anvil from two stainless steel ingots: put a second hot ingot on the work piece. The helve hammer forges it as it forges a plate, once both ingots are on. A large gear blank mold takes stainless steel only.
blockdesc-toolmold-*-raw-gearblank: Fire it in a pit kiln or a beehive kiln to make a gear blank mold.
blockdesc-toolmold-*-fired-gearblank: Takes 25 units of molten stainless steel and casts a stainless gear blank. Stainless steel only.
blockdesc-toolmold-*-raw-largegearblank: Fire it in a pit kiln or a beehive kiln to make a large gear blank mold.
blockdesc-toolmold-*-fired-largegearblan: Takes 200 units of molten stainless steel and casts a large stainless gear blank. Stainless steel only.
smex:blockdesc-toolmold-*-raw-pipe: Fire it in a pit kiln or a beehive kiln to make a pipe mold.
smex:blockdesc-toolmold-*-fired-pipe: Takes 100 units of molten iron or steel and casts two pipe sections of that metal.
castpipes-handbook-mold-text: Iron and steel pipe is cast, never forged: the pipe mold is the only way to it. Clay-form a raw pipe mold (a slab with a long trough and a core down its middle for the bore) from blue, red or fire clay and fire it in a pit kiln or a beehive kiln, as Steelmaking Expanded's other molds. Set the fired mold on Steelmaking Expanded's canal mold pedestal (sneak and rightmouse with the mold in hand) and open its pour (sprint and rightmouse): it draws 100 units, one ingot's worth, of molten iron from a blast furnace's canal or of steel from a Bessemer converter's, and casts two pipe sections of that metal. Once the metal has hardened, take the mold off with an empty hand (sneak and rightmouse), set it down and take the sections out; the mold stays. A crucible pours into it on the ground as into any tool mold. Band the sections into pipe on the crafting grid with nails and strips of their metal and a hammer: each section makes a straight pipe, so an ingot of iron or steel casts two pipes, as many as the draw bench makes from an ingot of copper or lead.
chutesection-handbook-text: The tube blank, in copper or lead, is two angles soldered together along both seams. Nothing else makes one: lay two angles of a metal on the crafting grid with two tin or silver solder bars and a soldering iron for one blank. Copper tube blanks make chutes: copper blanks in a chute's pattern, a tin or silver solder bar for each blank and a soldering iron. Lead blanks make no chutes. Copper and lead tube blanks make pipe sections: hammered over the mandrel on the mandrel station, a blank makes two pipe sections; drawn through a die on the draw bench, four.
itemdesc-angle-*: A half plate folded once across its middle, at a right angle, on the press brake. Two, soldered together with two solder bars and a soldering iron, make a tube blank.
angle-handbook-text: A copper or lead half plate folded once across its middle, at a right angle, the first piece of copper and lead pipe. Only the press brake makes one, from a half plate cut on the squaring shear: one half plate, one angle. Two angles of a metal, two tin or silver solder bars and a soldering iron make one tube blank on the crafting grid: the only way to one.
itemdesc-pipesection-*: A short length of pipe-sized tube. One makes a straight pipe; two, three or four a bend, T- or X-junction.
pipesection-handbook-text: A length of pipe, a block long, in copper, lead, iron or steel. No crafting grid or anvil makes one. Copper and lead pipe sections come from a tube blank of the metal: hammered over the mandrel on the mandrel station, two from a blank; drawn on the draw bench, four. Iron and steel pipe sections are cast, never forged: two from each ingot's worth of metal in a pipe mold on Steelmaking Expanded's canal mold pedestal. Pipe is made from them on the crafting grid, laid out as a chute is: one section alone makes a straight pipe, two as an elbow a bend, three as a T a T-junction and four as a cross an X-junction. Copper and lead sections are soldered, a tin or silver solder bar for each section and a soldering iron; iron and steel sections are banded with one nails and strips of their metal and a hammer.
blockdesc-gearcutter-frame-*: The bed and column of a mechanically powered gear cutter that cuts stainless gear blanks into stainless gears. Fit its parts one at a time, in order: the spindle, the feed screw, two eccentric gearboxes for the cam drums, the lift cam, the index, an injection valve, a Jonas gear assembly for the dividing head, a cutter kit and a temporal gear as the master.
itemdesc-gearcutterspindle: The cutter's spindle with its cone pulley and bevels. The first part fitted to a gear cutter frame.
itemdesc-gearcutterfeedscrew: A steel worm and clutch sleeve: it turns the gear cutter's camshaft once a tooth.
itemdesc-gearcutterliftcam: A forged steel cam and hub: it lifts the gear cutter's knee into the cut and drops it out.
itemdesc-gearcutterindex: Lever, pawls and shield: they step the gear cutter's dividing head one tooth at a time.
itemdesc-gearcutterkit-*: A formed steel cutter, one tooth of the rack. The gear cutter's wearing part: oil spares it.

gearcutter-kit-section-text: The gear cutter's wearing part. A kit cuts about 50 small gears with a full oil tank, fewer as the tank runs down, and breaks on the first gear cut dry. ctrl + rightmouse takes it back out, with what is left of it.
gearcutter-handbook-assembly-text: Place the frame where the machine has room: two blocks wide, two deep and two high. It runs away from you, the block you place being its front corner at ground level, on your right as you face it; the column is at the back. Then fit its parts with rightmouse, one at a time and only in this order: a spindle (two steel rods, two steel plates and metal parts), a feed screw (smithed from a steel ingot), two eccentric gearboxes for the feed and index cam drums, a lift cam (smithed from a steel ingot), the index (two steel rods, two steel plates and metal parts), an alternate injection valve for the oiler, an exquisite planetary gear or a difference gear assembly for the dividing head, a cutter kit (smithed from a steel ingot) and a master: a temporal gear or a large temporal gear. Look at the frame to see what it takes next. ctrl + rightmouse takes the cutter kit back out, with what is left of it; then a blank on the arbor; then the master. The other parts come back only when you break the frame, which drops every part, the kit with its wear, and the blank. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on an unfinished cutter fits its next part, with nothing taken from you.
gearcutter-handbook-work-text: Connect a turning axle to the back of the column, behind the block you placed, at ground level. It may turn either way. The cutter is a heavy load and only cuts while its shaft turns at a fair speed. The master decides the size. With the temporal gear it cuts a stainless gear blank into a stainless gear of 12 teeth; with the large temporal gear, a large stainless gear blank into a large stainless gear of 20. It refuses the other size: change the master over to cut the other. The master rolls on the rack and is never used up. Put a blank on the arbor with rightmouse, or stand a chest or hopper with blanks against the end nearest the block you placed: the running cutter takes them one at a time. Each tooth takes 12 turns of the shaft, so a small gear takes 144 and a large one 240. The finished gear goes into a chest standing against the far end, or drops there.
gearcutter-handbook-oil-text: The cutter has an oil tank like the other heavy machines (see Oiling machines): rightmouse with oil fills it, and the glass on the overarm shows its level. Each small gear uses 10 points of oil, a large one 20. Dry or oiled it takes the same power: the oil goes on the cutter, sprayed from the injection valve. The cutter kit loses 10 points a small gear with a full tank, more as the tank runs down: twice as much at half full, ten times at a tenth, and a large gear wears it 20/12 as much. With no oil at all, the gear being cut breaks the kit. A spent kit stops the machine until a new kit is fitted. Look at the cutter to see the wear and the kit's life. These figures are the defaults of GearCutterSettings and MachineOilSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.

itemdesc-drawdie-steel: A hardened steel ring the draw bench pulls a tube blank through, over the mandrel's plug, into pipe sections. Draws lead and copper.

drawbench-die-section-text: The draw bench's wearing part, fitted last. An iron die draws lead only; a steel die draws lead and copper. A die draws 100 tube blanks, losing a point for each, oiled or dry, and is gone when it is worn out. ctrl + rightmouse takes it back out, with what is left of it, while no tube blank is on the bench.
drawbench-handbook-assembly-text: Place the frame where the bench has room: one block wide, one high and four long. It runs away from you, the block you place being the die end. Then fit its parts with rightmouse, one at a time and only in this order: a consumately crafted gearbox for the clutch and change gear, two chains of iron, meteoric iron or steel for the endless drawing chain, a heavy bracket for the dog that grips the drawn section, two rods of iron, meteoric iron or steel for the mandrel and its follower, and a draw die: an iron die (two iron ingots at the anvil) or a steel die (two steel ingots). The chains and the rods go in two at a time, from one stack. Look at the frame to see what it takes next. ctrl + rightmouse takes the die back out, with what is left of it, while no tube blank is on the bench. The other parts come back only when you break the frame, which drops every part, the die with its wear, and a tube blank no pipe section has been drawn from yet. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on an unfinished bench fits its next part, with nothing taken from you.
drawbench-handbook-work-text: Connect a turning axle to the side of the far end, on your right as you look along the bench from the die end. It may turn either way. The bench only draws while its shaft turns at a fair speed. What it draws is a lead or copper tube blank. Put one on with rightmouse, or stand a chest or hopper with them in front of the die end: the running bench takes them one at a time. The blank goes on over the mandrel, and four strokes of the chain draw it out through the die, a quarter at each, into four pipe sections: a lead blank makes four lead pipe sections, a copper one four copper ones. Lead runs in the fast gear, about 1.4 turns of the shaft a pipe section; copper in the slow one, about 2.7. Each pipe section comes off as soon as it is drawn through the die, at the die end, on your left, or into a chest standing there. The die decides the metal: an iron die draws lead only, a steel die lead and copper. Each tube blank wears the die a point. From angle to pipe Two angles of a metal, two tin or silver solder bars and a soldering iron make a tube blank on the crafting grid. A tube blank makes two pipe sections hammered on the mandrel station, or four drawn here. A pipe section, a solder bar and a soldering iron make a straight pipe; two, three or four, with as many solder bars, a bend, T- or X-junction.
drawbench-handbook-oil-text: The bench has an oil tank like the other heavy machines (see Oiling machines): rightmouse with oil fills it, and the oiler's glass shows its level. Each pipe section drawn uses 2 points, a tube blank 8. Dry, it takes three times the power to turn, and smokes. These figures are the defaults of DrawBenchSettings and MachineOilSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.

Fit its parts one at a time, in order: metal parts for the clamp screws, then a plate for the wearing edges.

pressbrake-handbook-assembly-text: Place the frame where the brake has room: one block wide, one high and two long. It runs away from you, the block you place being the leaf end, where you stand to work it. Then fit its parts with rightmouse, one at a time and only in this order: metal parts, made up into the two clamp screws and their tommy bars, then a metal plate of iron or steel, cut into the wearing edges of the bed, the leaf and the clamping bar. Look at the frame to see what it takes next. Once fitted, the parts stay in: only breaking the frame gives them back. It drops every part, and a half plate not yet folded. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on an unfinished brake fits its next part, with nothing taken from you.
pressbrake-handbook-work-text: What it folds is a half plate: a lead half plate or a copper half plate, cut from a plate on the squaring shear. A whole plate does not go on. Put a half plate on the bed with rightmouse: it lies across the folding edge, half on the bed and half over the leaf. Then hold rightmouse on the brake to work it, as you turn a quern: it only folds while you hold. The screws bring the clamping bar down on the sheet, the leaf swings up and folds it once across its middle, at a right angle, and the bar is screwed up again: one half plate makes one angle. A lead half plate takes about a second and a half of work, a copper one, stiffer, about two and a quarter. The angle comes off over the leaf towards you, or into a chest standing in front of the leaf end. Stand a chest or hopper of half plates beyond the far end of the bed and the brake takes the next one from it whenever you work it with nothing on the bed, so you can keep holding from one to the next. ctrl + rightmouse takes a half plate back off while it is still flat; once folding has begun it stays on until it is done. The brake needs no power and no oil, and its edges do not wear. These figures are the defaults of PressBrakeSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.
pressbrake-handbook-ladder-text: Each half plate makes one angle, and nothing else makes one: a plate cut in two on the squaring shear makes two angles. Two angles of a metal, two tin or silver solder bars and a soldering iron make one tube blank on the crafting grid. Tube blanks make chutes, copper only, or pipe: hammered over the mandrel on the mandrel station a tube blank makes two pipe sections, drawn on the draw bench four, and pipe sections, soldered, make pipe.

It runs away from you, the block you place being the table end, where you stand to work it. Then fit its iron with rightmouse, one part at a time and only in this order: a metal plate of iron or steel, ground into the upper and lower blades, then a rod of iron, meteoric iron or steel, for the back gauge and the hold-down. squaringshear-handbook-work-text: What it cuts is a plate: a lead plate or a copper plate. Put one on the table with rightmouse, then hold rightmouse on the shear to work its treadle, as you turn a quern: it only cuts while you hold. The plate lies against the back gauge, the hold-down comes down on it, the treadle brings the blade down through it across its middle, and the two halves come back across the table towards you: one plate makes two half plates. A lead plate takes about a second of work, a copper one, stiffer, about a second and a half. The half plates come off in front of the table end, or into a chest standing there. Stand a chest or hopper of plates beyond the far end and the shear takes the next plate from it whenever you work it with nothing on the table, so you can keep holding from one plate to the next. ctrl + rightmouse takes a plate back off while it is still whole; once cutting has begun it stays on until it is done. cruciblefurnace-handbook-text: Made and used in the crucible furnace: see the Making stainless steel guide.
cruciblefurnace-text: Stainless steel is iron with about a seventh of chromium in it, and chromium is the trouble: it will not come out of its ore in a bloomery, and stainless melts at 1530 °C, hotter than coke burns in any forge. So it is made the Sheffield way, a little at a time, in pots in a crucible furnace. The furnace A melting hole is set into the floor: eight fired tier-3 refractory bricks round an iron plate, its lid. Holes stand in a row, up to four side by side, and the row needs a stack: a chimney of brick (clay bricks, refractory bricks or stone bricks) at one end, in line with the holes, from their level up at least 6 blocks. The flue runs under the floor. Look at a hole to see whether its row has its draft. The pot Clay-form a melting pot from fire clay and fire it in a pit kiln or a beehive kiln, as a crucible is fired. A pot holds 200 units, two ingots' worth, and lasts 3 heats: it cracks after its third. One pot goes in each hole. Charging Open the lid (Shift and right-click with an empty hand opens and shuts it), put a pot in, and right-click with the charge: as much goes in as the recipes allow. The pot knows its recipes only by their ratios, and takes nothing that would spoil every one of them: an ingot is 100 units, anything else 5. - Ferrosilicon: crushed quartz half (45-55 %), iron bits 25-35 %, coke 15-25 % (Shift and right-click to put coke in the pot, not on the fire). Melts at 1400 °C. A full pot, 20 quartz, 12 iron bits and 8 coke, gives 20 ferrosilicon. - Ferrochrome: crushed chromite half (45-55 %), ferrosilicon 25-35 %, lime 15-25 %: the silicon takes the oxygen from the chromite, and the lime takes the silica into slag. Melts at 1550 °C. A full pot, 20 chromite, 12 ferrosilicon and 8 lime, gives 20 ferrochrome and 8 slag. - Stainless steel: iron (ingots or bits; not steel, whose carbon would take the chromium) and ferrochrome, about 4 to 1 (ferrochrome 18-22 %). Melts at 1530 °C. A full pot: an iron ingot, 12 iron bits and 8 ferrochrome, 200 units of stainless. - Stainless remelt: stainless bits (or ingots) alone, 20 bits to 100 units. A charge that matches no recipe will not light, and the hole says what is off. Firing Coke only: right-click coke onto the fire, up to 6, each burning an hour. Light it with a firestarter or a torch, lid open, then shut the lid. On the chimney's draft alone a hole heats by about 200 °C an hour, up to 1600 °C: about 7 to 8 hours to stainless, so top the coke up on the way. Forced air is twice as fast and reaches 1650 °C, about 4 hours: run a Pipes and Power Expanded pipe carrying air from Steelmaking Expanded's twin-tub blower or steam air blower to the side of, or under, any hole of the row. An open lid or a fire out of coke cools the hole. Pulling and teeming When the charge has melted, open the lid and, with tongs in your off hand and an empty hand, right-click to pull the pot. Ferroalloys come out as their lumps, broken out of the pot. Stainless stays molten in the pot: pour it like a crucible into ingot molds or gear blank molds. You have about 20 seconds before it freezes in the pot; a frozen pot is lost, and right-clicking it knocks the metal out as stainless bits, which go back in the next pot. In bulk: the Bessemer converter Ferrochrome is also scrap for Steelmaking Expanded's Bessemer converter, charged at its hatch any time: with the raw iron before the blow, during it, or into the finished steel after it. If ferrochrome is 18-22 % of the heat's metal when it pours, the same 4 to 1 as in a pot, and the bath is at least 1530 °C, the heat pours molten stainless steel down the canal, into ingot molds or gear blank molds like any metal. Off the ratio, or too cold, it pours steel and the ferrochrome is lost to the slag. The vessel's panel shows the ferrochrome and what the heat will pour.

It runs away from you, the block you place being the stump, where you stand to work, with the mandrel pointing away. Then fit its mandrel with rightmouse: a rod of iron, meteoric iron or steel, held in the bracket. It stays in: only breaking the frame gives it back, with a tube blank not yet struck. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on a station with no mandrel fits an iron one, with nothing taken from you.
mandrelstation-handbook-work-text: What it forges is a lead or copper tube blank. Slip one over the mandrel with rightmouse, then strike it: each rightmouse with a hammer in hand is a blow, as on the anvil, and costs the hammer as much. The blows draw the metal out along the mandrel and close the box down onto it; at the last blow the smith parts it, and two pipe sections of its metal slide off the tip and drop beyond it, or into a chest standing there. With a copper hammer a lead blank takes nine blows, a copper one, harder, fourteen. A better hammer forges faster, in proportion to its tool tier: a bronze one takes six blows for lead and ten for copper, an iron or meteoric iron one five and seven, a steel one four and six. Stand a chest or hopper of tube blanks beside the stump and a blow on the bare mandrel takes the next one from it. Without one, keep rightmouse held as a blank is finished and the next blank of the same metal on your hotbar goes on by itself, so the hammering carries on. ctrl + rightmouse takes a blank back off before the first blow; once struck, it stays on until it is done. The station needs no power and no oil. These figures are the defaults of MandrelStationSettings in ModConfig/seraphhorizons.json.

itemdesc-handcar: A standard-gauge rail car for two, pumped by hand. Place it on standard-gauge track, step onto either end and pump the walking beam.
handcar-handbook-text: Place the handcar on standard-gauge track as you would a wagon. Two can ride, one at each end of the walking beam, facing each other across it: press rightmouse on the deck at either end to step on, and sneak to step off. Pumping Hold walkforward to pump the car the way you face, walkbackward to pump it the way your back is to. Let go and it coasts, slowing as it rolls. Pump against the way it rolls and it brakes to a stop before it starts back. One rider alone gets the car to about 4 blocks a second, two pumping together to about 6: each rider adds thrust, and the other only rides until they pump too. Two pumping against each other lock the beam. A chest on board, or a wagon coupled behind, slows it. Pumping is as hungry work as running. Switches Press walkleft or walkright to throw the branch selector beside the pump stand one place that way, as you face: left, straight on, right. The car takes that branch at the next switch, and the selector stays where it is put. Cargo The deck behind the rear rider takes a chest or a crate. Taking it up With nobody on board and the car stopped, press sneak and rightmouse with an empty hand to pick it up, or take it apart with a wrench, holding a hammer in your other hand. Either way it comes back whole.

Fit its winch in order, then hang the spine on its chain: eight wooden axles, a metal rod for the crank shaft, four spur gears, ten planks of its wood for the drum and sheave, ten nails and strips, a metal plate for the ratchet and pawl, a rod for the crank, four chains, and three support beams of its wood for the spine.

eidolongantry-handbook-build-text: The gantry is where an eidolon is built, and its dock afterwards. Its frame is crafted from 24 support beams of one wood, 16 nails and strips of iron, meteoric iron or steel, a hammer and a saw, with the eidolon schematic, which is kept; the gantry is of the beams' wood. It stands 6 blocks deep, 5 wide and 5 and a half high, with its open front towards you: the block you place it on is the middle of the front, on the ground. Everything it covers must be free. The crank turns outside it, on the left at the back, a block up, and needs that block free too. Then fit its winch with rightmouse, one stage at a time and only in this order, each stage taking all its items from the stack you hold at once: 1. 8 wooden axles: the layshaft and the drum's shaft 2. a rod of iron, meteoric iron or steel: the crank shaft 3. 4 spur gears: two lanterns and two cog wheels 4. 10 planks of the gantry's wood: the drum and the sheave 5. 10 nails and strips of iron, meteoric iron or steel: the hoops and collars 6. a plate of iron, meteoric iron or steel: the ratchet and pawl 7. a rod of iron, meteoric iron or steel: the crank 8. 4 chains of iron, meteoric iron or steel: the chain, its swivel eye and ring 9. 3 support beams of the gantry's wood: the spine, hung on the chain, on which the eidolon's body is built Look at the gantry to see what it takes next. Nothing comes back but by breaking the gantry, which drops the frame and everything fitted to it. With the spine hung, the eidolon's body is built on it, stage by stage: the torso, pelvis, legs, arms and head, each finished before the next, its items in any order. Each rightmouse fits what the stack you hold can give toward one item the stage still needs. The head takes the Eidolon elucidatory vessel from the Resonance Archives' eidolon, its brain. Last, the mind: a temporal gear, its first charge, wakes it. It is yours, steps down off the spine and walks out of the open front, and the gantry, its spine empty again, is ready to build another. In creative mode, ctrl + rightmouse on a gantry fits its next stage (the winch's, then the body's: the last wakes the eidolon), with nothing taken from you, and the creative inventory has an assembled oak gantry, its winch built and spine hung.

A tool commands up to 16 eidolons. Choose an order with toolmodeselect, then right-click anywhere else to give it to every eidolon the tool is bound to within reach (64 blocks, unless the server says otherwise): Follow me: it keeps a few blocks behind you, walking, or running to catch up. Where it can find no way to you (a gap it cannot cross, a door less than 2 blocks wide and 4 high) it stops, waits and tells you so, and comes on once it can. Stay here: it holds where it stands. Orders that work in a place have you mark it first: a block with one right-click, an area with two (opposite corners). The tool keeps each order's marks and shows them while you hold it; sneak and right-click to clear them.
